questions.question: Which of the following best defines a transverse river profile?
options: A cross-section showing the width and depth of a river channel and its valley.
A graph showing the relationship between a river's discharge and its velocity.
A side view of a river from its source in the mountains to its mouth at the sea.
A bird's eye view showing the drainage pattern of the entire river basin.

questions.question: What is the permanent base level of a river?
options: Sea level
A large, resistant outcrop of igneous rock
The level of the water table during the dry season
A large inland lake or dam

questions.question: A dam wall built across a river channel acts as a:
options: Temporary base level
Permanent base level
Source of river rejuvenation
Knickpoint of tectonic origin

questions.question: A graded river profile indicates a state of dynamic equilibrium. This means that:
options: The rate of erosion is equal to the rate of deposition.
The river only erodes its bed vertically and never laterally.
The river has completely stopped eroding and is only depositing sediment.
The river's velocity is constantly increasing from source to mouth.

questions.question: If you observe a longitudinal profile with multiple sharp drops in elevation (waterfalls), you are looking at an:
options: Ungraded profile
Graded profile
Over-graded profile
Equilibrium profile

questions.question: What is a 'knickpoint' on a longitudinal profile?
options: A sharp change in the gradient of the river bed, often indicating a temporary base level.
The lowest point the river can reach, which is always sea level.
A point where a tributary joins the main river channel.
The point in the upper course where the river starts flowing.

questions.question: River rejuvenation occurs when a river regains its ability to erode downwards. Which two factors primarily cause this?
options: A drop in sea level (eustatic change) or an uplift of the land (tectonic uplift).
An increase in sea level or a subsidence (sinking) of the land.
A decrease in rainfall leading to lower river discharge.
An increase in the sediment load from a tributary.

questions.question: When a river is rejuvenated, which type of erosion becomes dominant?
options: Vertical (downward) erosion
Lateral (sideways) erosion
Headward (backward) erosion
Wind erosion

questions.question: Which of the following landforms is a direct result of river rejuvenation?
options: Incised (entrenched) meanders
Oxbow lakes
Braided streams
Natural levees

questions.question: On a cross-sectional diagram of a rejuvenated river valley, what are the elevated, flat steps on either side of the new channel called?
options: River terraces
Flood plains
Slip-off slopes
Undercut banks

questions.question: What do river terraces represent?
options: The remnants of the river's older, higher flood plain before rejuvenation occurred.
Areas where recent floods have deposited new, fertile soil.
Man-made structures built to stop the river from flooding.
The lowest level the newly rejuvenated river can erode down to.

questions.question: When drawing a cross-section of an incised meander caused by rejuvenation, the valley sides should be drawn:
options: Steep and roughly symmetrical, indicating rapid downward erosion.
Very gentle and wide, indicating slow lateral erosion.
Completely flat, showing a wide flood plain.
Only steep on the outside curve, and completely flat on the inside curve.
